statement: A [rewriting system](c:rewriting-system) that is terminating ([strongly normalizing](c:strong-normalization)) and [locally confluent](c:locally-confluent-relation) is [confluent](c:confluence).

hypotheses.text: The relation $\to$ on the set $A$ is [terminating](c:strong-normalization): there is no infinite chain $a_0 \to a_1 \to a_2 \to \cdots$.
The relation is [locally confluent](c:locally-confluent-relation): if $a \to b$ and $a \to c$, then $b \to^* d$ and $c \to^* d$ for some $d$.

conclusion: The relation is [confluent](c:confluence): if $a \to^* b$ and $a \to^* c$, then $b \to^* d$ and $c \to^* d$ for some $d$.

proofs.name: Well-founded induction on the start point
proofs.slogan: Prove confluence at each element by well-founded induction along the terminating relation, and close each peak with local confluence and two induction hypotheses.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the converse, that confluence gives local confluence, holds for every relation. Peaks with $b = a$ or $c = a$ are settled separately in step 2.

roles.why: Termination makes $\to^+$ a well-founded relation, so the induction is valid.
Local confluence closes the one-step peak $b_1 \leftarrow a \to c_1$ at the top.

steps.slogan: Order the elements by $\to^+$ and set up [well-founded induction](c:well-founded-induction).
steps.detail: Because $\to$ terminates, $\to^+$ has no infinite chain, so induction along it is valid. Prove the claim $P(a)$: any two reducts $b, c$ of $a$ have a common reduct, assuming $P(a')$ for every $a'$ with $a \to^+ a'$.

steps.slogan: Settle the peaks where one side takes zero steps.
steps.detail: If $b = a$, then $c$ is a common reduct of $b$ and $c$, because $a \to^* c$. The case $c = a$ is symmetric.

steps.slogan: Split a nontrivial peak into first steps $a \to b_1$ and $a \to c_1$.
steps.detail: Otherwise $a \to b_1 \to^* b$ and $a \to c_1 \to^* c$. [Local confluence](c:locally-confluent-relation) gives $d$ with $b_1 \to^* d$ and $c_1 \to^* d$.

steps.slogan: Join $b$ and $d$ by the induction hypothesis at $b_1$.
steps.detail: Since $a \to^+ b_1$, the hypothesis $P(b_1)$ applies to the reducts $b$ and $d$ of $b_1$ and gives $e$ with $b \to^* e$ and $d \to^* e$.

steps.slogan: Join $c$ and $e$ by the induction hypothesis at $c_1$.
steps.detail: Both $c$ and $e$ are reducts of $c_1$, because $c_1 \to^* d \to^* e$. Since $a \to^+ c_1$, $P(c_1)$ gives $f$ with $c \to^* f$ and $e \to^* f$, so $b \to^* e \to^* f$.

steps.slogan: Combine both cases into $P(a)$ and conclude [confluence](c:confluence) by induction.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 5 give a common reduct of $b$ and $c$ in every case, so $P(a)$ holds. By well-founded induction $P(a)$ holds for every $a$, which is confluence.

concepts.c:rewriting-system: The lemma is about the reduction relation of a rewriting system.
concepts.c:strong-normalization: Termination makes the reduction relation usable for induction.
concepts.c:locally-confluent-relation: Local confluence closes the top peak of each diagram.
concepts.c:confluence: Confluence is the property proved at every element.
concepts.c:well-founded-induction: Induction along the reduction relation supplies the hypotheses at $b_1$ and $c_1$.

statement: For a [compact group](c:compact-group) $G$, the matrix coefficients $g \mapsto \langle \pi(g)u, v \rangle$ of finite-dimensional continuous [unitary representations](c:unitary-representation) $\pi$ span a [dense](c:dense-set) subspace of $C(G)$ in the sup norm.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a compact Hausdorff topological group.

conclusion: Every [continuous function](c:continuous-function) on $G$ is a uniform limit of finite linear combinations of matrix coefficients ([representative functions](c:representative-function)).

proofs.name: Compact convolution operators
proofs.slogan: Smooth a continuous function by a convolution operator, expand it in the finite-dimensional eigenspaces of that compact operator, and read the eigenfunctions as matrix coefficients.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including the trivial group. Density in $L^2(G)$ follows, because $C(G)$ is dense in $L^2(G)$.

roles.why: Compactness gives a finite [Haar measure](c:haar-measure), a compact convolution operator and uniform continuity of $f$.

steps.slogan: Convolve with a symmetric continuous kernel to get a [compact self-adjoint operator](c:compact-self-adjoint-operator).
steps.detail: Let $dy$ be the normalized [Haar measure](c:haar-measure). For continuous $\varphi$ with $\varphi(y^{-1}) = \overline{\varphi(y)}$, the [convolution](c:convolution) $Tf(x) = \int \varphi(xy^{-1}) f(y)\,dy$ has a bounded kernel on a finite measure space, so $T$ is self-adjoint and Hilbert-Schmidt, hence compact, on $L^2(G)$. It commutes with right translations $R_g f(x) = f(xg)$.

steps.slogan: Choose the kernel as a bump at the identity so that $\varphi * f$ is uniformly close to $f$.
steps.detail: Given $f \in C(G)$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, uniform continuity gives a symmetric neighborhood $U$ of $e$ with $|f(z^{-1}x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon$ for $z \in U$. Urysohn's lemma gives a symmetric continuous $\varphi \ge 0$ supported in $U$ with $\int \varphi = 1$, and then $\|\varphi * f - f\|_\infty < \varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Split $L^2(G)$ into the kernel of $T$ and finite-dimensional translation-invariant eigenspaces.
steps.detail: The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators gives $L^2(G) = \ker T \oplus \overline{\bigoplus_{\lambda \ne 0} E_\lambda}$ with each $E_\lambda$ finite dimensional. Each $E_\lambda$ is invariant under right translations because $T$ commutes with them, and its elements are continuous because $f = \lambda^{-1}\,\varphi * f$.

steps.slogan: Write each function of an invariant finite-dimensional space as a combination of matrix coefficients.
steps.detail: Right translation on $W = E_\lambda$ is a continuous [unitary representation](c:unitary-representation), because Haar measure is right invariant. For a basis $f_1, \dots, f_m$ of $W$, $f_i(xg) = \sum_j a_{ji}(g) f_j(x)$ with matrix coefficients $a_{ji}$, and $x = e$ gives $f_i = \sum_j f_j(e)\,a_{ji}$, a [representative function](c:representative-function).

steps.slogan: Truncate the eigen-expansion and control the error uniformly by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
steps.detail: Write $f = f_0 + \sum_\lambda f_\lambda$ in $L^2$ with $Tf_0 = 0$. Since $\|Th\|_\infty \le \|\varphi\|_2 \|h\|_2$, a finite partial sum $h$ of the $f_\lambda$ gives $\|Tf - Th\|_\infty < \varepsilon$; then $Th$ is a combination of matrix coefficients by step 4, and $\|f - Th\|_\infty < 2\varepsilon$ by step 2.

concepts.c:compact-group: Compactness of the group drives every step of the proof.
concepts.c:unitary-representation: Right translation on an eigenspace is a finite-dimensional unitary representation.
concepts.c:dense-set: The theorem asserts density of the span of matrix coefficients.
concepts.c:continuous-function: The functions approximated are the continuous functions on $G$.
concepts.c:representative-function: Matrix coefficients are the approximating functions.
concepts.c:haar-measure: The invariant probability measure defines convolution and the $L^2$ inner product.
concepts.c:compact-self-adjoint-operator: Its spectral theorem gives finite-dimensional eigenspaces.
concepts.c:convolution: Convolution with a bump smooths $f$ and defines the compact operator.

statement: Let $A, B, C$ be [finite sets](c:finite-set) in a group written additively, and suppose $|A+B|\,|A'| \le |A'+B|\,|A|$ for every $A' \subseteq A$. Then the [sumsets](c:sumset) satisfy $|C+A+B|\,|A| \le |A+B|\,|C+A|$.

hypotheses.text: The sets $A$, $B$ and $C$ are [finite](c:finite-set) subsets of a group $G$, written additively.
Every $A' \subseteq A$ has $|A+B|\,|A'| \le |A'+B|\,|A|$, so $A$ minimizes $|A'+B|/|A'|$ among its nonempty subsets.

conclusion: $|C+A+B|\,|A| \le |A+B|\,|C+A|$; for nonempty $A$ this reads $|C+A+B| \le K\,|C+A|$ with $K = |A+B|/|A|$.

proofs.name: Induction on C
proofs.slogan: Add the points of $C$ one at a time, and pay for each new translate $x + A$ only with the part that $C + A$ does not cover yet.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by induction on $|C|$; the group need not be commutative, so the sums keep their order. For empty $A$ or empty $C$ both sides are $0$.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the cardinalities numbers and allows induction on $|C|$.
Minimality bounds from below the part $A' + B$ that the new translate shares with old sums.

steps.slogan: Check the inequality for empty $C$, where both sides are zero.
steps.detail: If $C = \emptyset$, then $C + A + B$ and $C + A$ are empty, so both sides are $0$. For the induction step, assume the inequality for $C$ and let $C' = C \cup \{x\}$ with $x \notin C$.

steps.slogan: Define $A'$ as the points of $A$ whose translate by $x$ already lies in $C + A$.
steps.detail: Let $A' = \{a \in A : x + a \in C + A\}$, so $(x + A) \cap (C + A) = x + A'$. Then $x + A' + B \subseteq C + A + B$, and $C' + A + B = (C + A + B) \cup \big((x + A + B) \setminus (x + A' + B)\big)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the new [sumset](c:sumset) by $|C + A + B| + |A + B| - |A' + B|$.
steps.detail: The union bound and $x + A' + B \subseteq x + A + B$ give $|C'+A+B| \le |C+A+B| + |x+A+B| - |x+A'+B|$. Left [translation](c:translation) by $x$ is a bijection, so $|x + A + B| = |A + B|$ and $|x + A' + B| = |A' + B|$.

steps.slogan: Multiply by $|A|$ and apply the induction hypothesis and the minimality of $A$.
steps.detail: The induction hypothesis gives $|C+A+B|\,|A| \le |A+B|\,|C+A|$, and the hypothesis on $A$ gives $|A'+B|\,|A| \ge |A+B|\,|A'|$. So $|C'+A+B|\,|A| \le |A+B|\,(|C+A| + |A| - |A'|)$.

steps.slogan: Count $C' + A$ by inclusion-exclusion to close the induction.
steps.detail: Since $C' + A = (C + A) \cup (x + A)$ with intersection $x + A'$, we get $|C' + A| = |C + A| + |A| - |A'|$. With step 4 this gives $|C'+A+B|\,|A| \le |A+B|\,|C'+A|$.

concepts.c:finite-set: Finite sets have cardinalities, and induction runs over $|C|$.
concepts.c:sumset: The inequality compares sizes of sumsets.
concepts.c:translation: Translates $x + A$ have the same size as $A$.

statement: Let $A, B$ be [finite sets](c:finite-set) in an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) with $A$ nonempty and $|A+B| \le K|A|$. Then for all integers $m, n \ge 0$ the iterated [sumsets](c:sumset) satisfy $|mB - nB| \le K^{m+n}|A|$.

hypotheses.text: The sets $A$ and $B$ are [finite](c:finite-set) subsets of an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $G$.
The set $A$ is nonempty.
The [sumset](c:sumset) satisfies $|A+B| \le K|A|$.

conclusion: $|mB - nB| \le K^{m+n}|A|$, where $mB$ is the set of sums of $m$ elements of $B$.

formal.difference: The declaration takes $K = |A+B|/|A|$ exactly. A larger $K$ follows at once, because $K^{m+n}$ grows with $K$.

proofs.name: Petridis subset and Ruzsa triangle
proofs.slogan: Pass to a subset of $A$ with the least growth ratio, grow it by Petridis' inequality, and split the difference set by Ruzsa's triangle inequality.
proofs.scope: All $m, n \ge 0$; for $m = n = 0$ the set $\{0\}$ has size $1 \le |A|$. The proof needs $A \ne \emptyset$ for the ratios to exist.

roles.why: Finiteness gives a minimizing subset, and commutativity lets the proof reorder $X + (k-1)B + B$.
A nonempty $A$ has nonempty subsets, so the minimum ratio exists.
The bound $|A+B| \le K|A|$ caps the minimal ratio by $K$.

steps.slogan: Choose a nonempty $X \subseteq A$ that minimizes the ratio $|X+B|/|X|$.
steps.detail: The nonempty subsets of $A$ form a finite nonempty family because $A \ne \emptyset$, so some $X$ minimizes $|X+B|/|X|$. Set $K_X = |X+B|/|X|$; then $K_X \le |A+B|/|A| \le K$ and $|X| \le |A|$.

steps.slogan: Grow $X$ by one copy of $B$ at a time with the Plünnecke-Petridis inequality.
steps.detail: By the choice of $X$, the Plünnecke-Petridis inequality applies to $X$, $B$ and $C = (k-1)B$ and gives $|X + kB| \le K_X\,|X + (k-1)B|$. Induction on $k$ gives $|X + kB| \le K_X^{k}\,|X|$ for every $k \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Bound the difference set by Ruzsa's triangle inequality through $X$.
steps.detail: Ruzsa's triangle inequality gives $|mB - nB|\,|X| \le |X + mB|\,|X + nB|$: fix $d = b - b'$ for each $d \in mB - nB$, and the map $(d, x) \mapsto (x + b, x + b')$ is injective.

steps.slogan: Combine the two bounds and divide by $|X|$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $|mB - nB|\,|X| \le K_X^{m+n}\,|X|^2$, so $|mB - nB| \le K_X^{m+n}\,|X| \le K^{m+n}\,|A|$ by step 1.

concepts.c:finite-set: Finite sets give finite ratios and a minimizing subset.
concepts.c:abelian-group: Commutativity lets the proof reorder iterated sums.
concepts.c:sumset: The inequality bounds the size of iterated sumsets.

statement: Let $T$ be a [measure-preserving map](c:measure-preserving-map) of a space $X$ with a [finite measure](c:finite-measure) $\mu$, and let $A$ be a [measurable set](c:measurable-set). Then [almost every](c:almost-everywhere) point $x \in A$ returns to $A$ infinitely often: $T^n x \in A$ for infinitely many $n$.

hypotheses.text: The measure $\mu$ is [finite](c:finite-measure): $\mu(X) < \infty$.
The map $T\colon X \to X$ is measurable and [measure preserving](c:measure-preserving-map): $\mu(T^{-1}E) = \mu(E)$ for every measurable $E$.
The set $A$ is [measurable](c:measurable-set).

conclusion: The points $x \in A$ with $T^n x \in A$ for only finitely many $n$ form a [null set](c:null-set).

formal.difference: The declaration assumes only that $T$ is conservative, a wider class that contains every measure-preserving map of a finite measure space (MeasurePreserving.conservative). It also allows null-measurable sets.

proofs.name: Conservativity and a last return time
proofs.slogan: Find returning points in every set of positive measure, upgrade this to returns at arbitrarily late times, and show that late non-returners form null sets.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the case $\mu(A) = 0$ is trivial. Steps 1 and 2 prove that $T$ is conservative, the hypothesis of the mathlib theorem.

roles.why: A finite total measure cannot hold $N$ almost disjoint sets of measure $\mu(E)$ when $N\mu(E) > \mu(X)$.
Preimages keep the measure $\mu(E)$, and measurability of $T$ keeps the sets $B_n$ measurable.
Measurability of $A$ makes each set $B_n$ measurable.

steps.slogan: Find a returning point in every set of positive measure by pigeonhole on its preimages.
steps.detail: Let $\mu(E) > 0$ and choose $N$ with $N\mu(E) > \mu(X)$. The sets $T^{-k}E$, $0 \le k < N$, all have measure $\mu(E)$, so some $T^{-i}E \cap T^{-j}E$ with $i < j$ has positive measure. It equals $T^{-i}(E \cap T^{-(j-i)}E)$, so some $x \in E$ has $T^{j-i}x \in E$.

steps.slogan: Show by contradiction that $\mu(E \cap T^{-m}E) > 0$ for infinitely many $m$.
steps.detail: Otherwise let $N$ be the largest such $m$ (with $m = 0$ allowed) and remove from $E \cap T^{-N}E$ the null sets $E \cap T^{-n}E$, $n > N$. Step 1 applied to the remaining set $F$ gives $x \in F$ and $k \ge 1$ with $T^k x \in F$. Then $x \in E$ and $T^{N+k}x \in E$, against $x \notin E \cap T^{-(N+k)}E$.

steps.slogan: Show that the points of $A$ that never return after time $n$ form a null set.
steps.detail: Let $B_n = \{x \in A : T^m x \notin A \text{ for all } m \ge n\}$, a measurable set. If $\mu(B_n) > 0$, step 2 gives $m \ge n$ and $x \in B_n$ with $T^m x \in B_n \subseteq A$, which contradicts $x \in B_n$.

steps.slogan: Take the countable union of the null sets $B_n$.
steps.detail: A point of $A$ that returns only finitely often lies in some $B_n$. The union $\bigcup_n B_n$ is a countable union of [null sets](c:null-set), so [almost every](c:almost-everywhere) $x \in A$ returns infinitely often.

concepts.c:measure-preserving-map: Preimages under the map keep their measure.
concepts.c:finite-measure: A finite total measure cannot hold too many sets of equal positive measure.
concepts.c:measurable-set: The returning set and its preimages must be measurable.
concepts.c:almost-everywhere: The theorem holds outside a set of measure zero.
concepts.c:null-set: The exceptional points form a countable union of null sets.

proofs.name: Equal measure of tail sets
proofs.slogan: Compare the set of points that visit $A$ at some time $n \ge N$ with its preimage, and use that both have the same finite measure.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, without the notion of a conservative map.

roles.why: Finiteness allows the subtraction $\mu(A_0) - \mu(A_N)$.
Measure preservation gives $\mu(T^{-N}A_0) = \mu(A_0)$.
Measurability of $A$ and of $T$ makes the tail sets measurable.

steps.slogan: Define the tail sets $A_N = \bigcup_{n \ge N} T^{-n}A$ of points that visit $A$ at a time $n \ge N$.
steps.detail: Each $A_N$ is a [measurable set](c:measurable-set), $A \subseteq A_0$, the sets decrease in $N$, and $T^{-N}A_0 = A_N$.

steps.slogan: Show that every tail set has the same measure as $A_0$.
steps.detail: Measure preservation gives $\mu(A_N) = \mu(T^{-N}A_0) = \mu(A_0)$. Since $A_N \subseteq A_0$ and $\mu(A_0) < \infty$, $\mu(A_0 \setminus A_N) = \mu(A_0) - \mu(A_N) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the points of $A$ outside a tail set form a null set.
steps.detail: Since $A \subseteq A_0$, the set $A \setminus A_N$ lies in $A_0 \setminus A_N$, so $\mu(A \setminus A_N) = 0$ for every $N$.

steps.slogan: Intersect over $N$ to get the points that return infinitely often.
steps.detail: A point $x \in A$ returns infinitely often exactly when $x \in \bigcap_N A_N$. The exceptional set $A \setminus \bigcap_N A_N = \bigcup_N (A \setminus A_N)$ is a countable union of [null sets](c:null-set), so it is null.

concepts.c:measure-preserving-map: Preservation gives each tail set the measure of $A_0$.
concepts.c:finite-measure: Finite measure lets equal measures of nested sets give a null difference.
concepts.c:measurable-set: The tail sets are measurable because $A$ is.
concepts.c:almost-everywhere: The theorem holds outside a set of measure zero.
concepts.c:null-set: The exceptional set is a countable union of null sets.

source.note: The classical tail-set proof, as in P. Walters, An Introduction to Ergodic Theory, chapter 1.

statement: For every measurable $\mu\colon \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ with $\|\mu\|_\infty < 1$, the [Beltrami equation](c:beltrami-equation) $\partial_{\bar z} f = \mu\,\partial_z f$ has exactly one [quasiconformal](c:quasiconformal-map) [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) solution $f\colon \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ in the [Sobolev space](c:sobolev-space) $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with $f(0) = 0$ and $f(1) = 1$.

hypotheses.text: The coefficient $\mu$ is a [measurable function](c:measurable-function) on $\mathbb{C}$.
The coefficient satisfies $\|\mu\|_\infty \le k < 1$.

conclusion: There is exactly one quasiconformal homeomorphism $f$ of $\mathbb{C}$ with $f(0) = 0$, $f(1) = 1$ and $\partial_{\bar z} f = \mu\,\partial_z f$ almost everywhere.

proofs.name: Beurling transform and Neumann series
proofs.slogan: Invert $I - \mu T$ for the Beurling transform $T$ on $L^p$, build the solution from the Cauchy transform, and prove that it is a unique homeomorphism.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the $L^p$ bound of the Beurling transform and the homeomorphism property rest on the cited work. Steps 2 to 4 assume that $\mu$ has compact support.

roles.why: Measurability makes $\mu h$ a function in $L^p$, so the operator $h \mapsto \mu T h$ acts on $L^p$.
The bound $k < 1$ with $C_p \to 1$ makes $\mu T$ a contraction for some $p > 2$, and it bounds the distortion of the approximating maps.

steps.slogan: Bound the Beurling transform $T$ on $L^p$ with norm $C_p \to 1$ as $p \to 2$.
steps.detail: The Cauchy transform $Ph$ satisfies $\partial_{\bar z} Ph = h$, and $Th = \partial_z Ph$ is a singular integral that is an isometry of $L^2$. Calderón-Zygmund theory bounds $T$ on every $L^p$, $1 < p < \infty$, and Riesz-Thorin interpolation gives $C_p \to 1$ as $p \to 2$.

steps.slogan: Solve $h = \mu T h + \mu$ by a Neumann series for compactly supported $\mu$.
steps.detail: Choose $p > 2$ with $k\,C_p < 1$. Then $h \mapsto \mu T h$ is a contraction of $L^p$, so $h = \sum_{j \ge 0} (\mu T)^j \mu$ converges, and $h$ has compact support with $\mu$.

steps.slogan: Set $f(z) = z + Ph(z)$ and check the [Beltrami equation](c:beltrami-equation).
steps.detail: Then $\partial_{\bar z} f = h$ and $\partial_z f = 1 + Th$, so $\partial_{\bar z} f = \mu\,\partial_z f$. Since $h \in L^p$ with $p > 2$, $f$ lies in the [Sobolev space](c:sobolev-space) $W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and is Hölder continuous.

steps.slogan: Approximate $\mu$ by smooth coefficients to show that $f$ is a homeomorphism.
steps.detail: For smooth compactly supported $\mu_n \to \mu$ with $\|\mu_n\|_\infty \le k$, the solutions $f_n$ are diffeomorphisms. The cited work shows that the $f_n$ and their inverses are equicontinuous and converge uniformly, so $f$ is a quasiconformal [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism).

steps.slogan: Remove the support condition by the reflection $z \mapsto 1/z$ and a composition.
steps.detail: Split $\mu$ into its parts inside and outside the unit disc. The cited work conjugates the outer part by $z \mapsto 1/z$ to a compactly supported coefficient, solves it, solves for the coefficient of the remaining factor, and normalizes the composition to fix $0$ and $1$.

steps.slogan: Prove uniqueness, since two normalized solutions differ by a conformal map that fixes $0$ and $1$.
steps.detail: If $f$ and $g$ are normalized solutions, $g \circ f^{-1}$ is a $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ homeomorphism with $\partial_{\bar z} = 0$, so Weyl's lemma makes it conformal on $\mathbb{C}$. Such a map is $az + b$, and the normalization makes it the identity; with step 5 this gives exactly one solution.

concepts.c:beltrami-equation: The theorem solves this equation for every admissible coefficient.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The solution must be a bijective continuous map with continuous inverse.
concepts.c:sobolev-space: The solution has locally integrable weak derivatives.
concepts.c:measurable-function: Only measurability and a bound are asked of the coefficient.

statement: Let $k$ be a field or a [principal ideal domain](c:principal-ideal-domain) and $n \ge 0$. Every finitely generated [projective module](c:projective-module) over the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is [free](c:free-module).

hypotheses.text: The coefficient ring $k$ is a field or a [principal ideal domain](c:principal-ideal-domain).
The module $P$ is finitely generated and [projective](c:projective-module) over $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$.

proofs.name: Horrocks' theorem and Quillen patching
proofs.slogan: Induct on the number of variables: invert monic polynomials, use the induction hypothesis there, and descend freeness by Horrocks' theorem and Quillen patching.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; Horrocks' theorem and the patching theorem rest on the cited work. The case $n = 0$ is the structure theorem over a principal ideal domain.

roles.why: A principal ideal domain gives free modules at $n = 0$ and stays principal after inverting monic polynomials.
Finite generation and projectivity are the hypotheses of Horrocks' theorem, of patching and of the induction hypothesis.

steps.slogan: Settle $n = 0$ by the structure theorem over a principal ideal domain.
steps.detail: A finitely generated projective module over $k$ is a direct summand of some $k^m$, so it is torsion free. The structure theorem makes it [free](c:free-module).

steps.slogan: Prove Horrocks' theorem: over a [local ring](c:local-ring), freeness after inverting monic polynomials gives freeness.
steps.detail: For a local ring $R$ and a finitely generated projective $R[t]$-module $P$, the cited work shows that $P$ is free if $P$ becomes free after inverting all [monic polynomials](c:monic-polynomial) of $R[t]$.

steps.slogan: Patch local extendedness to global extendedness by Quillen's patching theorem.
steps.detail: If $P_{\mathfrak m}$ is extended from $R_{\mathfrak m}$ for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $R$, then $P \cong (P/tP) \otimes_R R[t]$. With step 2: if $P$ becomes free after inverting the monic polynomials of $R[t]$, then $P$ is extended from $R$.

steps.slogan: Invert the monic polynomials in $x_n$ over $k$ and apply the induction hypothesis.
steps.detail: The [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) $k\langle x_n \rangle$ of $k[x_n]$ at its monic polynomials is again a field or a principal ideal domain. Over it, $P$ becomes a finitely generated projective module over a polynomial ring in $n - 1$ variables, so it is free by induction.

steps.slogan: Descend freeness to $P$ through $R = k[x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}]$ and $t = x_n$.
steps.detail: Monic polynomials in $x_n$ over $k$ are monic over $R$, so $P$ is free after inverting the monic polynomials of $R[x_n]$, and step 3 gives $P \cong P_0 \otimes_R R[x_n]$ with $P_0 = P/x_nP$. The module $P_0$ is finitely generated projective over $R$, free by induction, so $P$ is free.

concepts.c:principal-ideal-domain: Over a PID, projective modules are free, which starts the induction.
concepts.c:projective-module: The theorem shows that these modules are free.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The induction removes one variable of the polynomial ring at a time.
concepts.c:free-module: Freeness is the conclusion at every stage of the induction.
concepts.c:local-ring: Horrocks' theorem works over a local base ring.
concepts.c:monic-polynomial: Inverting monic polynomials gives the ring where freeness is known.
concepts.c:localization-of-a-ring: The proof passes to localizations at monic polynomials and at maximal ideals.

statement: Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be open, $c \in U$, and let $f$ be [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $U \setminus \{c\}$ and [bounded](c:bounded-function) on a [punctured neighborhood](c:punctured-neighborhood) of $c$. Then $\lim_{z \to c} f(z)$ exists, and $f$ extended by this value is holomorphic on $U$.

hypotheses.text: The set $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is open and contains $c$.
The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $U \setminus \{c\}$.
The function $f$ is [bounded](c:bounded-function) on $\{z : 0 < |z - c| < r\}$ for some $r > 0$.

conclusion: The limit $L = \lim_{z \to c} f(z)$ exists, and the function equal to $f$ off $c$ and to $L$ at $c$ is holomorphic on $U$.

formal.difference: The declaration assumes only $f(z) - f(c) = o(1/(z - c))$ as $z \to c$, which boundedness implies. It allows values in a complex Banach space.

proofs.name: Multiply by z - c and divide
proofs.slogan: Multiply by $z - c$ to get a function that is continuous at $c$, show that it is analytic there, and divide the factor back out.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the value at $c$ is $F'(c)$, which is the limit of $f$.

roles.why: Openness gives a closed disc around $c$ inside $U$.
Holomorphy off $c$ makes $F$ holomorphic off $c$ and the extension holomorphic away from $c$.
Boundedness makes $F(z) = (z - c) f(z)$ tend to $0$, so $F$ is continuous at $c$.

steps.slogan: Form $F(z) = (z - c) f(z)$ and set $F(c) = 0$.
steps.detail: $F$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $U \setminus \{c\}$ as a product of holomorphic functions. Since $|f| \le M$ near $c$, $|F(z)| \le M|z - c| \to 0$, so $F$ is continuous at $c$.

steps.slogan: Represent $F$ by the Cauchy integral formula on a disc around $c$.
steps.detail: On a closed disc $\bar D \subseteq U$ around $c$, $F$ is continuous and holomorphic except at the single point $c$. The Cauchy-Goursat theorem still holds for such a function, so the Cauchy integral formula holds on $D$ and $F(z) = \sum_{k \ge 0} a_k (z - c)^k$ there.

steps.slogan: Divide the power series by $z - c$, using $a_0 = F(c) = 0$.
steps.detail: Since $a_0 = F(c) = 0$, the [power series](c:power-series) $g(z) = \sum_{k \ge 0} a_{k+1}(z - c)^k$ is holomorphic on $D$, and $g(z) = F(z)/(z - c) = f(z)$ for $z \ne c$.

steps.slogan: Define $f(c) = g(c)$ and check holomorphy on all of $U$.
steps.detail: Then $\lim_{z \to c} f(z) = g(c) = a_1 = F'(c)$ exists. The extended function equals $g$ on $D$ and $f$ on $U \setminus \{c\}$, so it is holomorphic on $U$.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy off $c$ is what the extension upgrades to all of $U$.
concepts.c:bounded-function: Boundedness near $c$ is the condition that removes the singularity.
concepts.c:punctured-neighborhood: The bound is only asked on a punctured neighborhood of $c$.
concepts.c:power-series: A power series expansion around $c$ defines the extension.

proofs.name: Square factor and Taylor series
proofs.slogan: Multiply by $(z - c)^2$ to get a function with value and derivative zero at $c$, and expand it in a Taylor series.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; it uses that a function complex differentiable on an open set is analytic.

roles.why: Openness gives a disc around $c$ inside $U$ for the Taylor series.
Holomorphy off $c$ makes $h$ holomorphic off $c$ and the extension holomorphic away from $c$.
Boundedness gives $|h(z)| \le M|z - c|^2$, so $h'(c) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Form $h(z) = (z - c)^2 f(z)$ and set $h(c) = 0$.
steps.detail: $h$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $U \setminus \{c\}$ as a product of holomorphic functions. Because $f$ is [bounded](c:bounded-function) by $M$ near $c$, $|h(z)| \le M|z - c|^2$ there.

steps.slogan: Show that $h$ is complex differentiable at $c$ with $h'(c) = 0$.
steps.detail: The difference quotient is $(h(z) - h(c))/(z - c) = (z - c) f(z)$, of modulus at most $M|z - c| \to 0$. So $h'(c) = 0$, and $h$ is holomorphic on all of $U$.

steps.slogan: Expand $h$ in its Taylor series around $c$, whose first two coefficients vanish.
steps.detail: A holomorphic function is analytic by the Cauchy integral formula, so $h(z) = \sum_{k \ge 0} a_k (z - c)^k$ on a disc $D \subseteq U$ around $c$. Here $a_0 = h(c) = 0$ and $a_1 = h'(c) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Divide by $(z - c)^2$ and define $f(c) = a_2$.
steps.detail: On $D \setminus \{c\}$, $f(z) = \sum_{k \ge 0} a_{k+2}(z - c)^k$, a [power series](c:power-series) that is holomorphic on $D$. So $\lim_{z \to c} f(z) = a_2$, and $f$ extended by $a_2$ is holomorphic on $U$.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy off $c$ is what the extension upgrades to all of $U$.
concepts.c:bounded-function: Boundedness near $c$ is the condition that removes the singularity.
concepts.c:punctured-neighborhood: The bound is only asked on a punctured neighborhood of $c$.
concepts.c:power-series: A power series expansion around $c$ defines the extension.

statement: Fix a [Gödel numbering](c:godel-numbering) $e \mapsto \varphi_e$ of the [partial computable functions](c:partial-computable-function). For every total [computable function](c:computable-function) $f$ from codes to codes, some code $c$ satisfies $\varphi_{f(c)} = \varphi_c$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f$ from codes to codes is total and [computable](c:computable-function).

conclusion: There is a code $c$ such that $c$ and $f(c)$ compute the same partial function.

formal.difference: The declaration uses mathlib's own coding Nat.Partrec.Code, with evaluation Code.eval, as the numbering.

proofs.name: Diagonal code by currying
proofs.slogan: Build codes that run the output of a self-application, compose them with $f$, and feed that composite its own code.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the proof uses only a universal evaluator and the s-m-n theorem (currying) of the numbering.

roles.why: Totality and computability of $f$ make $f \circ d$ a total computable function with a code $v$.

steps.slogan: Define the partial computable function $g(x, y) = \varphi_{\varphi_x(x)}(y)$.
steps.detail: Run program $x$ on input $x$; if it halts with output $b$, run program $b$ on $y$. A universal program evaluates codes computably, so $g$ is [partial computable](c:partial-computable-function) and has a code $e$.

steps.slogan: Curry the code $e$ to get codes $d(x)$ with $\varphi_{d(x)}(y) = g(x, y)$.
steps.detail: The s-m-n theorem gives a primitive recursive map $x \mapsto d(x)$ with $\varphi_{d(x)}(y) = g(x, y) = \varphi_{\varphi_x(x)}(y)$ for all $y$. In mathlib, $d(x)$ is the code curry $e$ $x$.

steps.slogan: Compose $f$ with $d$ and take a code $v$ of the total function $f \circ d$.
steps.detail: The map $x \mapsto f(d(x))$ is total and [computable](c:computable-function) because $f$ and $d$ are. So it has a code $v$ with $\varphi_v(x) = f(d(x))$ for all $x$.

steps.slogan: Take $c = d(v)$ and unfold both sides to get $\varphi_{f(c)} = \varphi_c$.
steps.detail: For every $y$, $\varphi_c(y) = \varphi_{d(v)}(y) = \varphi_{\varphi_v(v)}(y)$ by step 2, and $\varphi_v(v) = f(d(v)) = f(c)$ halts. So $\varphi_c(y) = \varphi_{f(c)}(y)$ for all $y$.

concepts.c:godel-numbering: Programs are coded by numbers, so a program can receive its own code.
concepts.c:partial-computable-function: The function $g$ and every $\varphi_e$ are partial computable functions.
concepts.c:computable-function: The map $f$ must be total and computable to have a code.

statement: Let $S$ be a finite set of relations on $\{0, 1\}$. The [satisfiability](c:boolean-satisfiability) problem $\mathrm{SAT}(S)$ for conjunctions of $S$-constraints is in P if all relations of $S$ are 0-valid, or all 1-valid, Horn, dual Horn, bijunctive (2-CNF) or affine (linear over $\mathbb{F}_2$); otherwise it is [NP-complete](c:np-complete).

hypotheses.text: The constraint language $S$ is a finite set of relations on $\{0, 1\}$.

conclusion: $\mathrm{SAT}(S)$ is solvable in polynomial time in the six listed cases and [NP-complete](c:np-complete) in every other case.

proofs.name: Polymorphisms and pp-definitions
proofs.slogan: Match the six tractable classes to six polymorphisms, and show that a language without them pp-defines an NP-complete relation.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the classification of idempotent Boolean clones in step 5 rests on the cited work. Instances have no constants; constants appear only inside the hardness reduction.

roles.why: Finiteness makes each constraint checkable in constant time and keeps the pp-definitions of fixed size.

steps.slogan: Place $\mathrm{SAT}(S)$ in NP by guessing and checking an assignment.
steps.detail: An assignment of the variables is a certificate of polynomial size, and each constraint is checked in constant time because $S$ is finite. So $\mathrm{SAT}(S)$ is in [NP](c:np-complexity-class).

steps.slogan: Solve each of the six classes in polynomial time with its own algorithm.
steps.detail: A constant assignment satisfies every 0-valid or 1-valid instance. Unit propagation decides Horn and dual Horn instances, the implication graph decides 2-CNF instances, and Gaussian elimination over $\mathbb{F}_2$ decides affine instances.

steps.slogan: Characterize the six classes by the [polymorphisms](c:polymorphism) $0$, $1$, $\wedge$, $\vee$, majority and $x \oplus y \oplus z$.
steps.detail: A relation is Horn exactly when it is closed under coordinatewise $\wedge$, dual Horn under $\vee$, bijunctive under majority and affine under $x \oplus y \oplus z$. The 0-valid and 1-valid cases are the constant polymorphisms.

steps.slogan: Reduce $\mathrm{SAT}(R)$ to $\mathrm{SAT}(S)$ when every polymorphism of $S$ preserves $R$.
steps.detail: By the [Galois connection](c:galois-connection) between relations and operations, such an $R$ has a primitive positive definition from $S$ and equality. Replacing each $R$-constraint by this definition, with fresh existential variables, is a polynomial-time reduction.

steps.slogan: Show that a language with none of the six polymorphisms pp-defines an NP-complete relation.
steps.detail: Without constant polymorphisms, $S$ pp-defines the constants or is closed under negation. The cited work shows that an idempotent Boolean [clone](c:clone) without $\wedge$, $\vee$, majority and minority holds only projections, so $S$ pp-defines 3-SAT clauses or not-all-equal 3-SAT.

steps.slogan: Combine the algorithms and the hardness reduction into the dichotomy.
steps.detail: If $S$ lies in one of the six classes, step 2 solves $\mathrm{SAT}(S)$ in polynomial time. Otherwise $S$ has none of the six polymorphisms by step 3, and steps 1, 4 and 5 make $\mathrm{SAT}(S)$ [NP-complete](c:np-complete).

concepts.c:boolean-satisfiability: The problems classified are restricted Boolean satisfiability problems.
concepts.c:np-complete: Every language outside the six classes gives an NP-complete problem.
concepts.c:np-complexity-class: Membership in NP is half of NP-completeness.
concepts.c:polymorphism: The six tractable classes are exactly the languages with six polymorphisms.
concepts.c:galois-connection: Polymorphisms determine which relations a language pp-defines.
concepts.c:clone: Polymorphisms of a language form a clone, and clones are classified.

statement: Let $H$ be a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of a group $G$, let $R$ be a set of right [coset representatives](c:coset-representatives) of $H$ with $1 \in R$, write $\bar g \in R$ for the representative of $Hg$, and let $S$ be a [generating set](c:generating-set) of $G$. Then $H$ is generated by the elements $rs\,(\overline{rs})^{-1}$ with $r \in R$ and $s \in S$.

hypotheses.text: The set $R$ contains exactly one element of each right coset $Hg$, and $1 \in R$.
The set $S$ [generates](c:generating-set) $G$.

proofs.name: Closure of the transversal products
proofs.slogan: Show that the Schreier generators lie in $H$, that their subgroup times $R$ is all of $G$, and read off $H$ from the unique decomposition.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; $G$, $S$ and $R$ may be infinite. The normalization $1 \in R$ is used in the last step.

roles.why: The transversal supplies the representatives $\bar g$ and, with $1 \in R$, the unique decomposition $g = hr$.
Generation by $S$ lets right multiplications by $S \cup S^{-1}$ reach every element.

steps.slogan: Check that each Schreier generator lies in $H$.
steps.detail: For $g \in G$, $g$ and $\bar g$ lie in the same right [coset](c:coset) $Hg$, so $g\,\bar g^{-1} \in H$. In particular $rs\,(\overline{rs})^{-1} \in H$, and the [subgroup](c:subgroup) $U$ these elements generate lies in $H$.

steps.slogan: Show that $UR$ is closed under right multiplication by each $s \in S$.
steps.detail: For $u \in U$ and $r \in R$, $urs = u\,\big(rs\,(\overline{rs})^{-1}\big)\,\overline{rs}$, and the middle factor is a Schreier generator. So $urs \in UR$.

steps.slogan: Show that $UR$ is closed under right multiplication by each $s^{-1}$.
steps.detail: Let $r' = \overline{rs^{-1}}$. Then $r's \in Hr$, so $\overline{r's} = r$, and $urs^{-1} = u\,\big(r's\,(\overline{r's})^{-1}\big)^{-1} r' \in UR$.

steps.slogan: Generate $G$ from $1 \in UR$ by right multiplications with $S \cup S^{-1}$.
steps.detail: Every element of $G$ is a product $s_1^{\pm 1} \cdots s_k^{\pm 1}$ because $S$ is a [generating set](c:generating-set). Starting from $1 = 1 \cdot 1 \in UR$, steps 2 and 3 give $UR = G$ by induction on $k$.

steps.slogan: Decompose $h \in H$ as $ur$ and force $r = 1$ by uniqueness.
steps.detail: By step 4, $h = ur$ with $u \in U \subseteq H$ and $r \in R$. Then $r = u^{-1}h \in H$ represents the coset $H$, so $r = 1$ because $1 \in R$; hence $h = u$ and $U = H$.

concepts.c:subgroup: The lemma gives generators of the subgroup $H$.
concepts.c:coset-representatives: The representatives build the generators and give unique decompositions.
concepts.c:generating-set: Generators of $G$ produce the Schreier generators of $H$.
concepts.c:coset: An element and its representative lie in the same right coset.

statement: Let $V$ and $W$ be [irreducible representations](c:irreducible-representation) of a group $G$ over a field $k$. Every $G$-equivariant linear map ([module homomorphism](c:module-homomorphism)) $\varphi\colon V \to W$ is zero or an isomorphism. If $k$ is [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field) and $V$ is finite dimensional, every $G$-equivariant $\varphi\colon V \to V$ is a scalar $\lambda\,\mathrm{id}$.

hypotheses.text: The representations $V$ and $W$ are nonzero and [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation).
The linear map $\varphi$ commutes with the action: $\varphi(gv) = g\,\varphi(v)$ for all $g \in G$.
For the second part, the field $k$ is [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field).
For the second part, $V$ is finite dimensional over $k$.

conclusion: A $G$-map between irreducible representations is $0$ or invertible, and under the extra hypotheses every $G$-endomorphism of $V$ is a scalar multiple of the identity.

formal.difference: The declaration proves the second part only, as $\dim_k \mathrm{End}(X) = 1$ for a simple object $X$ of a $k$-linear category with kernels and finite-dimensional endomorphisms. The first part is CategoryTheory.isIso_of_hom_simple.

proofs.name: Kernel, image and an eigenvalue
proofs.slogan: Kernel and image of a $G$-map are subrepresentations, so the map is zero or invertible, and an eigenvalue turns any endomorphism into a scalar.
proofs.scope: Part one holds over any field and in any dimension. Part two needs both extra hypotheses: rotations of $\mathbb{R}^2$ commute with the rotation group but are not scalars.

roles.why: Irreducibility leaves only $0$ and the whole space as kernel and image.
Equivariance makes kernel and image $G$-stable and keeps $\varphi - \lambda\,\mathrm{id}$ equivariant.
Algebraic closure gives a root of the characteristic polynomial.
Finite dimension gives a characteristic polynomial of positive degree.

steps.slogan: Show that the kernel and the image of $\varphi$ are [subrepresentations](c:subrepresentation).
steps.detail: If $\varphi(v) = 0$, then $\varphi(gv) = g\,\varphi(v) = 0$, so $\ker\varphi$ is $G$-stable. Likewise $g\,\varphi(v) = \varphi(gv)$ shows that $\operatorname{im}\varphi$ is $G$-stable.

steps.slogan: Force the kernel and the image to be zero or everything by irreducibility.
steps.detail: By irreducibility, $\ker\varphi$ is $0$ or $V$, and $\operatorname{im}\varphi$ is $0$ or $W$. If $\varphi \ne 0$, then $\ker\varphi = 0$ and $\operatorname{im}\varphi = W$, so $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Pick an [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) $\lambda$ of an equivariant endomorphism $\varphi\colon V \to V$.
steps.detail: Since $V$ is finite dimensional and nonzero, the characteristic polynomial of $\varphi$ has positive degree. It has a root $\lambda \in k$ because $k$ is [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field), so $\varphi - \lambda\,\mathrm{id}$ is not injective.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi - \lambda\,\mathrm{id}$ is zero by the first part.
steps.detail: The map $\varphi - \lambda\,\mathrm{id}$ is $G$-equivariant and not an isomorphism, so step 2 makes it zero. Hence $\varphi = \lambda\,\mathrm{id}$, and with step 2 both parts hold.

concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Irreducibility leaves no proper nonzero kernel or image.
concepts.c:module-homomorphism: An equivariant linear map is a homomorphism of $k[G]$-modules.
concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: Algebraic closure supplies the eigenvalue in part two.
concepts.c:subrepresentation: Kernel and image are subrepresentations, so irreducibility applies to them.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: Subtracting an eigenvalue gives a non-invertible equivariant map.

statement: For a complex vector space $V$ of dimension $d$, the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group) $GL(V)$ and the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $S_n$ act on the [tensor power](c:tensor-power) $V^{\otimes n}$, each spanning the other's [commutant](c:commutant), and $V^{\otimes n} \cong \bigoplus_\lambda S_\lambda(V) \otimes M_\lambda$ over partitions $\lambda$ of $n$ with at most $d$ rows, with [Specht modules](c:specht-module) $M_\lambda$ and distinct [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation) $GL(V)$-modules $S_\lambda(V)$.

hypotheses.text: The space $V$ is a complex vector space of finite dimension $d$.

conclusion: The images of $\mathbb{C}[GL(V)]$ and $\mathbb{C}[S_n]$ in $\mathrm{End}(V^{\otimes n})$ are each other's commutants, and $V^{\otimes n}$ decomposes as stated.

proofs.name: Double centralizer
proofs.slogan: Show that the symmetric group algebra acts semisimply, identify its commutant with the span of the $g^{\otimes n}$, and decompose by the double centralizer theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $n \ge 1$; for $n = 0$ both sides are $\mathbb{C}$. Characteristic $0$ gives semisimplicity, and the infinite field gives density of $GL(V)$ in $\mathrm{End}(V)$.

roles.why: Characteristic zero gives semisimplicity, the infinite field gives density of $GL(V)$, and the dimension $d$ bounds the rows.

steps.slogan: Show that the image $B$ of $\mathbb{C}[S_n]$ in $\mathrm{End}(V^{\otimes n})$ is a [semisimple algebra](c:semisimple-algebra).
steps.detail: By Maschke's theorem, $\mathbb{C}[S_n]$ is semisimple because $n!$ is invertible in $\mathbb{C}$. A quotient of a semisimple algebra is semisimple, so $B$ is semisimple.

steps.slogan: Identify the [commutant](c:commutant) of $B$ with the symmetric tensors in $\mathrm{End}(V)^{\otimes n}$.
steps.detail: Under $\mathrm{End}(V^{\otimes n}) = \mathrm{End}(V)^{\otimes n}$, conjugation by a permutation permutes the tensor factors. So an operator commutes with $B$ exactly when it is a symmetric tensor in $\mathrm{End}(V)^{\otimes n}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the operators $g^{\otimes n}$ with $g \in GL(V)$ span the symmetric tensors.
steps.detail: Polarization writes each symmetrized $X_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes X_n$ through coefficients of $(t_1X_1 + \cdots + t_nX_n)^{\otimes n}$, so the $X^{\otimes n}$ span. A linear functional that vanishes on all $g^{\otimes n}$ is a polynomial in $X$ that vanishes where $\det X \ne 0$, hence everywhere.

steps.slogan: Decompose $V^{\otimes n}$ by the double centralizer theorem for $B$ and its commutant $A$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 show that the span $A$ of the $g^{\otimes n}$ is the commutant of $B$, and semisimplicity of $B$ makes $B$ the commutant of $A$. Then $V^{\otimes n} \cong \bigoplus_\lambda \mathrm{Hom}_{S_n}(M_\lambda, V^{\otimes n}) \otimes M_\lambda$, and Schur's lemma makes the nonzero spaces $S_\lambda(V) = \mathrm{Hom}_{S_n}(M_\lambda, V^{\otimes n})$ distinct irreducible $A$-modules.

steps.slogan: Show that the [Specht module](c:specht-module) $M_\lambda$ occurs exactly when $\lambda$ has at most $d$ rows.
steps.detail: With a Young symmetrizer $c_\lambda$, $M_\lambda \cong \mathbb{C}[S_n]\,c_\lambda$ and $S_\lambda(V) \cong c_\lambda V^{\otimes n}$. The column antisymmetrizer kills $V^{\otimes n}$ when a column is longer than $d$; otherwise $c_\lambda$ is nonzero on the tensor of basis vectors with $e_i$ in row $i$.

concepts.c:general-linear-group: Its diagonal action $g^{\otimes n}$ spans one of the two commutants.
concepts.c:symmetric-group: It permutes tensor factors and gives the other commutant.
concepts.c:tensor-power: Both groups act on the tensor power $V^{\otimes n}$.
concepts.c:commutant: The two algebras are each other's commutants.
concepts.c:specht-module: Specht modules are the irreducible $S_n$-modules that label the summands.
concepts.c:semisimple-algebra: Semisimplicity of $B$ makes the double centralizer theorem apply.

statement: Let $E_1, E_2, \dots$ be [independent](c:independence) events for a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $P$ with $\sum_n P(E_n) = \infty$. Then the [limit superior](c:limsup-of-sets) has $P(\limsup_n E_n) = 1$: [almost surely](c:almost-everywhere) infinitely many of the events occur.

hypotheses.text: The events $E_n$ are measurable and mutually [independent](c:independence).
The series $\sum_n P(E_n)$ diverges.

conclusion: The event $\limsup_n E_n = \bigcap_N \bigcup_{n \ge N} E_n$ has probability $1$.

proofs.name: Conditional Borel-Cantelli of Lévy
proofs.slogan: Express the limsup event through the sum of conditional probabilities given the past, and replace them by plain probabilities using independence.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; it rests on Lévy's extension of the Borel-Cantelli lemma, proved with martingales. The index shift drops $E_1$, which changes the sum by at most $1$.

roles.why: Independence makes each conditional probability given the past equal to the plain probability.
Divergence of the plain sum makes the conditional sum infinite almost everywhere.

steps.slogan: Let $\mathcal{F}_k$ be the [filtration](c:filtration) generated by the first $k$ events.
steps.detail: Set $\mathcal{F}_k = \sigma(E_1, \dots, E_k)$ for $k \ge 1$, an increasing family of $\sigma$-algebras. Consider the [conditional expectations](c:conditional-expectation) $P(E_{k+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_k)$ of the next event given the past.

steps.slogan: Identify $\limsup_n E_n$ almost surely with divergence of the conditional probabilities.
steps.detail: Lévy's extension of the Borel-Cantelli lemma states that, up to a null set, $\limsup_n E_n = \{\omega : \sum_{k \ge 1} P(E_{k+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_k)(\omega) = \infty\}$. It follows from martingale convergence applied to $\sum_{k \ge 1} \big(1_{E_{k+1}} - P(E_{k+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_k)\big)$.

steps.slogan: Replace each conditional probability by $P(E_{k+1})$ using independence.
steps.detail: Since $E_{k+1}$ is [independent](c:independence) of $\mathcal{F}_k$, $P(E_{k+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_k) = P(E_{k+1})$ almost surely. This holds for all $k$ at once off a null set, because there are countably many $k$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the sum diverges almost surely, so the limsup event has probability one.
steps.detail: The sum $\sum_{k \ge 1} P(E_{k+1})$ diverges because $\sum_n P(E_n)$ diverges and $P(E_1) \le 1$. So the set in step 2 is [almost all](c:almost-everywhere) of the space, and $P(\limsup_n E_n) = 1$.

concepts.c:probability-measure: The events live in a space with a probability measure.
concepts.c:limsup-of-sets: The limsup event is the event that infinitely many $E_n$ occur.
concepts.c:almost-everywhere: The conclusion holds outside an event of probability zero.
concepts.c:filtration: The past events generate the filtration of the martingale argument.

proofs.name: Product bound on the complement
proofs.slogan: Bound the probability that no event occurs after time $N$ by a product of the factors $1 - P(E_n)$, which tends to zero.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, through complements; it uses $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for real $x$.

roles.why: Independence of the complements factors the probability of their intersection.
Divergence of every tail sum drives the exponential bound to zero.

steps.slogan: Write the complement of $\limsup_n E_n$ as the union of the events $\bigcap_{n \ge N} E_n^c$.
steps.detail: A point lies outside $\limsup_n E_n$ exactly when it lies in only finitely many $E_n$, that is, in $\bigcap_{n \ge N} E_n^c$ for some $N$. So it suffices to show $P(\bigcap_{n \ge N} E_n^c) = 0$ for each $N$.

steps.slogan: Factor the probability of a finite intersection of complements by independence.
steps.detail: The complements $E_n^c$ are also [independent](c:independence), so $P(\bigcap_{n=N}^{M} E_n^c) = \prod_{n=N}^{M} (1 - P(E_n))$ for every $M \ge N$.

steps.slogan: Bound the product by $\exp(-\sum_{n=N}^{M} P(E_n))$, which tends to zero.
steps.detail: The inequality $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ gives $\prod_{n=N}^{M} (1 - P(E_n)) \le \exp(-\sum_{n=N}^{M} P(E_n))$. The tail sum diverges, so the bound tends to $0$ as $M \to \infty$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the decreasing limit in $M$ and take the countable union over $N$.
steps.detail: Continuity from above gives $P(\bigcap_{n \ge N} E_n^c) = \lim_M P(\bigcap_{n=N}^{M} E_n^c) = 0$. A countable union of null events is null, so $\limsup_n E_n$ holds [almost surely](c:almost-everywhere).

statement: For a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space) $X$, taking continuous [sections](c:section) $E \mapsto \Gamma(E)$ is an [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories) from real or complex [vector bundles](c:vector-bundle) of finite rank over $X$ to finitely generated [projective modules](c:projective-module) over the ring $C(X)$ of [continuous functions](c:continuous-function).

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is [compact and Hausdorff](c:compact-hausdorff-space).

conclusion: Every finitely generated projective $C(X)$-module is isomorphic to $\Gamma(E)$ for some vector bundle $E$, and bundle maps $E \to F$ correspond bijectively to module maps $\Gamma(E) \to \Gamma(F)$.

proofs.name: Complements and idempotent matrices
proofs.slogan: Embed each bundle as a summand of a trivial bundle to get projective modules, show that module maps act fiberwise, and build bundles from idempotent matrices.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the rank may vary between components of $X$. Compactness gives finite covers, and for noncompact $X$ the module $\Gamma(E)$ need not be finitely generated.

roles.why: Compactness gives a finite trivializing cover, and the Hausdorff property with compactness gives partitions of unity.

steps.slogan: Make $\Gamma(E)$ a $C(X)$-module and turn bundle maps into module maps.
steps.detail: [Sections](c:section) add pointwise and are multiplied by [continuous functions](c:continuous-function) pointwise, so $\Gamma(E)$ is a $C(X)$-module. A bundle map $E \to F$ composes with sections and gives a $C(X)$-linear map $\Gamma(E) \to \Gamma(F)$.

steps.slogan: Embed $E$ in a trivial bundle $X \times \mathbb{K}^N$ and split off a complement.
steps.detail: Finitely many trivializing open sets cover the [compact](c:compact-hausdorff-space) space $X$, and a [partition of unity](c:partition-of-unity) glues the local frames into an injective bundle map $E \to X \times \mathbb{K}^N$. The fiberwise orthogonal complement gives $E \oplus E^\perp \cong X \times \mathbb{K}^N$, so $\Gamma(E) \oplus \Gamma(E^\perp) \cong C(X)^N$.

steps.slogan: Show that a module map sends sections that vanish at $x$ to sections that vanish at $x$.
steps.detail: By step 2, $s = \sum_j a_j\,p(e_j)$ with the projections $p(e_j)$ of the constant frame and $a_j = \langle s, e_j \rangle \in C(X)$. If $s(x) = 0$, then all $a_j(x) = 0$, so $\varphi(s)$ vanishes at $x$; hence $\varphi$ comes from a unique continuous bundle map, and $\Gamma$ is fully faithful.

steps.slogan: Realize a finitely generated projective module as the image of an idempotent matrix.
steps.detail: If $P \oplus Q \cong C(X)^N$, the projection onto $P$ is an [idempotent](c:idempotent) matrix $p$ with entries in $C(X)$, and $P \cong p\,C(X)^N$.

steps.slogan: Build the bundle with fibers $E_x = p(x)\,\mathbb{K}^N$ and check that its sections form $P$.
steps.detail: The rank of $p(x)$ equals its trace, a continuous integer-valued function, so it is locally constant; near $x_0$ the vectors $p(x)v_i$ for a basis $v_i$ of $E_{x_0}$ stay a basis of $E_x$. So $E$ is a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle), and $\Gamma(E) = \{s : ps = s\} = p\,C(X)^N \cong P$.

steps.slogan: Combine full faithfulness and essential surjectivity into an equivalence.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 show that $\Gamma$ takes values in finitely generated [projective modules](c:projective-module) and is fully faithful. Steps 4 and 5 show that every such module is isomorphic to some $\Gamma(E)$, so $\Gamma$ is an [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories).

concepts.c:section: Continuous sections turn a bundle into a module.

concepts.c:continuous-function: The ring $C(X)$ of continuous functions acts on sections.
